title: Information decoys improve animal engagement with management devices
content:

Abstract

Effective pest management and wildlife monitoring often depend on animals engaging with management devices, yet animals often choose not to engage. While human decision-making can be influenced by altering choice context (choice architecture), whether similar approaches can improve wildlife engagement with conservation management devices remains largely unexplored. We tested whether phantom decoys, a type of information decoy consisting of an unavailable but highly desirable food cue, could nudge decision-making in a globally significant pest, the black rat (Rattus rattus), to improve device engagement rates. Placing phantom decoys outside the entrances of tracking tunnels in bushland habitats increased rat entry by 83% for tunnels containing low-quality bait. This pattern is consistent with predictions from phantom decoy theory. Synthesis and applications. Our findings suggest that simple choice architecture interventions can increase engagement with wildlife management devices and offer a novel strategy for improving wildlife detection and pest control outcomes.
